:::{#thm-eigen-idempotent-orthogonal}
#### Eigenvalues of idempotent and orthogonal matrices

1. Every eigenvalue of an idempotent matrix (@def-idempotent-matrix) is $0$ or $1$.
2. Every eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix (@def-orthogonal-matrix) is $1$ or $-1$.

:::

::: proof

Let $\vecf{v} \ne \vzero$ with $\matr{A} \vecf{v} = \eigval \vecf{v}$.

**Part 1.** If $\matr{A}^2 = \matr{A}$, then

$$
\ba
\eigval \vecf{v}
&= \matr{A} \vecf{v}
&& \text{(eigenvector)}
\\
&= \matr{A}^2 \vecf{v}
&& \text{(idempotent)}
\\
&= \eigval^2 \vecf{v},
&& \text{(@thm-eigen-shift-power, part 2)}
\ea
$$

and subtracting $\eigval \vecf{v}$ from both sides gives $(\eigval^2 - \eigval)\,\vecf{v} = \vzero$.
Some entry of $\vecf{v}$ is nonzero, so $\eigval^2 - \eigval = \eigval\,(\eigval - 1) = 0$,
and a product of two numbers is $0$ only when one of them is: $\eigval = 0$ or $\eigval = 1$.

**Part 2.** If $\matr{A}$ is orthogonal, then

$$
\ba
\norm{\vecf{v}}
&= \norm{\matr{A} \vecf{v}}
&& \text{(@thm-orthogonal-norm)}
\\
&= \norm{\eigval \vecf{v}}
&& \text{(eigenvector)}
\\
&= \abs{\eigval}\,\norm{\vecf{v}},
&& \text{(@thm-norm-properties, part 2)}
\ea
$$

and $\norm{\vecf{v}} > 0$ (@thm-norm-properties, part 1),
so dividing by $\norm{\vecf{v}}$ gives $\abs{\eigval} = 1$;
since $\eigval$ is real (@def-eigenvalue), $\eigval = 1$ or $\eigval = -1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-eigen-idempotent-orthogonal}
#### Projections and reflections

- The idempotent matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}$ of @exm-hat-matrix-projection
  sends $(1, 1)$ to $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ to $(0, 0)$: eigenvalues $1$ and $0$.
- The matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$, which swaps the two entries,
  is orthogonal: its columns $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ are orthonormal (@rem-orthogonal-matrix-columns).
  It sends $(1, 1)$ to $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ to $(-1, 1)$:
  eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$.
- The rotation $\matr{Q}$ of @exm-orthogonal-matrix has no real eigenvalue.
  By part 2 the only candidates are $\pm 1$.
  $\matr{Q} \vecf{v} = \vecf{v}$ reads $-0.4\,v_1 - 0.8\,v_2 = 0$ and $0.8\,v_1 - 0.4\,v_2 = 0$,
  so $v_1 = -2 v_2$ and $v_2 = 2 v_1 = -4 v_2$, forcing $\vecf{v} = \vzero$;
  $\matr{Q} \vecf{v} = -\vecf{v}$ reads $1.6\,v_1 - 0.8\,v_2 = 0$ and $0.8\,v_1 + 1.6\,v_2 = 0$,
  so $v_2 = 2 v_1$ and $0.8\,v_1 + 3.2\,v_1 = 0$, forcing $\vecf{v} = \vzero$ again.

:::
